title: Control pests, diseases and weeds on all crops effectively and responsibly

lessons.title: Recognising insects, diseases and weeds
lessons.html:
Know your enemies

To protect a crop you must first know what is attacking it. Pests, diseases and weeds all lower yield and quality, which means less money for the farm.

Common insect pests

PestCrop (examples)What you see
AphidsVegetables, citrus, wheatSmall soft insects in groups on new growth; sticky honeydew; curled leaves
Fall armyworm and stalk borerMaize, sorghumHoles in leaves, sawdust-like frass in the whorl, holes in stems
BollwormTomatoes, cotton, maizeCaterpillars and holes in fruit or cobs
Red spider miteBeans, tomatoes, fruit treesTiny mites under leaves, fine webbing, speckled yellow leaves
Fruit fly / false codling mothCitrus, deciduous fruitSting marks and rotting fruit, larvae inside

Remember: not all insects are pests. Ladybirds, lacewings and bees are friends of the farmer. Do not report them as pests.

Signs of disease

  • Spots on leaves or fruit (brown, black, yellow or with rings).
  • Powdery or furry growth (mildew, mould).
  • Wilting even when the soil is wet.
  • Rot on stems, roots or fruit.
  • Yellowing, mottling or curling (sometimes viruses).

Weeds

Learn the common names of the weeds in your fields, for example blackjack, pigweed (misbredie), nutgrass, khakibos, thorn apple (stinkblaar) and couch grass. Weeds steal water, food and light from the crop, and some, like thorn apple, are poisonous. Report new or unknown weeds too.

Report what you see

If you are not sure what a pest, disease or weed is, do not guess. Mark the plant with a flag or tape, write down the block and row, and show your supervisor. A photo on a phone can also help the farm manager or adviser identify it.

lessons.title: Scouting, damage and checking control results
lessons.html:
Scouting

Scouting means walking through the field in a set pattern and checking plants for pests, diseases and weeds. Your supervisor tells you the pattern and how many plants to check.

  1. Walk the pattern, for example a W or zigzag through the block. Do not only check the edges.
  2. Check the set number of plants at each stop: the top, the underside of leaves, the stem, fruit and the soil around the base.
  3. Count what you see and write it on the scouting sheet, with the block number and date.
  4. Check traps if there are any, and record the count.
  5. Report hot spots straight away.

Old or new damage?

The farmer must know whether the problem is still active.

New (active) damageOld damage
Fresh, green edges on chewed leavesDry, brown edges
Live insects or caterpillars presentNo insects, or only dead ones
Fresh, moist frass (droppings)Dry, old frass
Spots still spreading onto new leavesOnly old leaves affected; new growth clean

Report both, but say clearly which it is.

After spraying or other control

Scout the block again at the time your supervisor says. If the pest levels have not gone down, report it. Possible reasons you can mention:

  • the product did not reach the pest (poor coverage, pest under leaves),
  • rain washed it off,
  • the wrong product or dose was used,
  • the pest was at a stage that the product does not kill,
  • the pest has become resistant.

Safety

Never enter a sprayed block before the re-entry time on the sign. Wear long sleeves and a hat, and wash your hands before eating.

Key points

  • Learn the common pests, disease symptoms and weeds of your crop.
  • Not every insect is a pest: protect ladybirds and bees.
  • Scout in a set pattern, check the whole plant and record counts.
  • Tell old damage from new damage.
  • Report when pest levels do not drop after control.
